哉吁成王其賢也已考之無逸召誥諸篇所以
punctuated:
謂：「天命不易，而敬以保之，爾之儆予者深矣！予雖未能，豈無勉求之志哉？誠以德本明也，然人欲日爲之蔽錮，則天理遂至於晦蒙；學所以明也，然道心暫涉於忽忘，則人心即投其空隙。必也德欲日躋，而涵養操存不違於瞬息；學務時敏，而省察克治罔間於幾微。以日而言，必有就焉，所以求益於得者，固惟日之不足也；以月而言，必有將焉，所以引伸而長者，每計月而有餘也。法乾之健，而繼續有常，勿替自新之力；昭晉之明，而終始惟一，務收丕顯之功。克明俊德，雖非可易能也，于是積之以漸，而使蔽者通焉，庶乎心有所主，而所謂虛靈不昧者，可以復其體矣。敢怠焉而不脩乎？懋昭大德，雖非可易及也，于是持之以久，而使微者著焉，庶乎物無所淆，而所謂明覺自然者，可以達其用矣。敢畫焉而不進乎？夫然，則不聰可化，而敬止可幾；命雖不易，或可以保之而不失矣。不然，寧不負爾之望哉？」
吁！成王其賢也已！考之《無逸》《召誥》諸篇，所以
translation_en:
…saying: “Heaven’s Mandate is not easy to preserve, and reverence is the means of preserving it: profound indeed is your admonition to me! Though I have not yet attained this, how could I lack the resolve to strive for it? Virtue is indeed inherently luminous. Yet when human desires daily obscure and confine it, heavenly principle becomes shrouded in darkness. Learning is the means of illuminating it. Yet if the moral mind lapses even briefly into neglect or forgetfulness, the human mind immediately exploits the opening. Thus, if virtue is to rise daily, nourishment and vigilant preservation of the mind must not cease for an instant; if learning is to be pursued with timely diligence, scrutiny and self-mastery must leave no gap even in the subtlest stirrings of thought. Each day must bring an achievement: in seeking to add to what has already been gained, one indeed finds the day insufficient. Each month must bring progress: in extending and developing what has been gained, one finds an increase whenever the month is reckoned. Emulate the vigor of the Qian hexagram, continuing steadfastly without slackening the effort of self-renewal; manifest the brightness of the Jin hexagram, remaining consistent from beginning to end and striving to achieve splendid illumination. Being able to make illustrious one’s eminent virtue is no easy accomplishment. Yet by gradually accumulating effort and opening up what has been obstructed, one may give the mind a governing focus, so that what is called its empty, numinous, and unobscured character can be restored in its essential constitution. Would I dare grow idle and fail to cultivate it? Vigorously making great virtue manifest is no easy attainment. Yet by sustaining effort over time and bringing what is faint into prominence, one may prevent external things from causing confusion, so that what is called the mind’s natural clarity and awareness can fully exercise its functioning. Would I dare set limits for myself and cease advancing? In this way, lack of understanding can be transformed, and abiding in reverence can be approached. Though the Mandate is not easy to preserve, perhaps I can retain it without losing it. Otherwise, would I not disappoint your hopes?”
Ah! Worthy indeed was King Cheng! Examining such chapters as “Against Idleness” (Wu yi) and “The Announcement of the Duke of Shao” (Shao gao), the means by which…

title: 嘉靖三十七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
勉成王之敬德者不一而足敬之之說固即周
召數公之意與成王不惟味乎其言而且能致
乎其實此其所以克成厥德而基命宥密益衍
靈長之祚者也然諸書所稱惟恐君之不勉而
是詩所言惟恐臣之不吾勉合而觀之則其相
成之美可以想見而祈天永命之道誠無出此
也夫

translation_en:
…the exhortations urging King Cheng to revere virtue are too numerous to enumerate. Surely the teaching of “Be Reverent” (Jing zhi) expresses precisely the intentions of the dukes of Zhou and Shao and the other lords? King Cheng not only savored their words but also put them into practice. This was how he perfected his virtue and, laying the foundations of the mandate with magnanimity and quiet diligence, further extended his enduring blessed reign. Yet the various documents speak out of concern lest the ruler fail to exert himself, whereas this poem speaks out of concern lest his ministers fail to encourage him. Read together, they allow us to envision the beauty of ruler and ministers bringing one another to fulfillment. Truly, there is no better way to petition Heaven for an everlasting mandate!

Spring and Autumn Annals
“In winter, Gongsun Xia of Zheng led an army to attack Chen.” Twenty-fifth year of Duke Xiang.
“Shusun Bao met at Guo with Zhao Wu of Jin, Prince Wei of Chu, Guo Ruo of Qi, Xiang Xu of Song, Qi E of Wei, Prince Zhao of Chen, Gongsun Guisheng of Cai, Han Hu of Zheng, and representatives of Xu and Cao.” First year of Duke Zhao.

Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor: In recounting events recorded in the Classic, choosing the wording is difficult: some accounts are prolix without being clear; others are vague and lack substance. This composition is both detailed and accurate in its treatment of events, and its writing is refined and elegant. It also achieves the proper method of judgment and arrangement. It should be recorded as a model.
Comment by Examiner Gao, Reader-in-Waiting: Clear and orderly, with no empty words.
Comment by Examiner Dong, Academician: Accurate in its treatment of events and polished in expression.

title: 嘉靖三十七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
賢臣兩當乎強國由其能自立也此鄭有子產
而晉楚之強不能加也賢人之足以自立也如
是哉吾聞晉藉累霸之餘北方之國莫強焉鄭
處其南蓋惴惴焉承順之恐後者也方公孫夏
伐陳而子產之獻捷也侵小之問戎服之詰將
曲鄭而加之兵矣使無人以應之鄭能免乎幸
而子產將命原成周之大德而表先君之大惠
棄我懿親數陳罪也多焦數圻屈晉辭也各復
舊職申王命也其氣直其詞順雖以士莊伯之
===
辨無所復施而犯順不祥遂動趙文之悟矣不
然壤地千里之晉索賦而起禍且不可測也而
况肯受鄭之捷哉至若楚以僭王之夷南方之
國莫強焉鄭邇其北蓋恐恐焉聽命之不遑者
也方于虢之未會而子圍之圖婚也入館之舉
衆逆之謀將掩鄭而奪之國矣使無人以禦之
鄭其殆乎幸而子產授辭明小國之無辜而責
大國以安靖請墠于外抑其驕也包藏禍心發
其奸也距違君命申其鑒也其義正其詞嚴雖

賢臣兩當乎強國由其能自立也此鄭有子產
而晉楚之強不能加也賢人之足以自立也如
是哉吾聞晉藉累霸之餘北方之國莫強焉鄭
處其南蓋惴惴焉承順之恐後者也方公孫夏
伐陳而子產之獻捷也侵小之問戎服之詰將
曲鄭而加之兵矣使無人以應之鄭能免乎幸
而子產將命原成周之大德而表先君之大忠
棄我懿親數陳罪也多無數圻屈晉辭也各復
舊職申王命也其氣直其詞順雖以士莊伯之
===
辨無所復施而犯順不祥遂動趙文之悟矣不
然壤地千里之晉索賦而起禍且不可測也而
况肯受鄭之捷哉至若楚以僭王之夷南方之
國莫強焉鄭邇其壯蓋恐恐焉聽命之不遑者
也方于虢之未會而子圍之圖婚也入館之舉
衆逆之謀將掩鄭而奪之國矣使無人以禦之
鄭其殆乎幸而子產授辭明小國之無辜而責
大國以安靖請墠于外抑其驕也包藏禍心發
其奸也距違君命申其鑒也其義正其詞嚴雖
punctuated: 賢臣兩當乎強國，由其能自立也。此鄭有子產，而晉楚之強不能加也。賢人之足以自立也，如是哉！吾聞晉藉累霸之餘，北方之國莫強焉。鄭處其南，蓋惴惴焉承順之恐後者也。方公孫夏伐陳，而子產之獻捷也，侵小之問、戎服之詰，將曲鄭而加之兵矣。使無人以應之，鄭能免乎？幸而子產將命，原成周之大德，而表先君之大惠。「棄我懿親」，數陳罪也；「多焦數圻」，屈晉辭也；「各復舊職」，申王命也。其氣直，其詞順，雖以士莊伯之辨，無所復施，而「犯順不祥」，遂動趙文之悟矣。不然，壤地千里之晉，索賦而起禍，且不可測也，而况肯受鄭之捷哉！至若楚，以僭王之夷，南方之國莫強焉。鄭邇其北，蓋恐恐焉聽命之不遑者也。方于虢之未會，而子圍之圖婚也，入館之舉、衆逆之謀，將掩鄭而奪之國矣。使無人以禦之，鄭其殆乎？幸而子產授辭，明小國之無辜，而責大國以安靖。「請墠于外」，抑其驕也；「包藏禍心」，發其奸也；「距違君命」，申其鑒也。其義正，其詞嚴，雖
translation_en:
That a worthy minister can stand against two powerful states rests on his ability to hold his ground. Thus Zheng had Zichan, and the might of Jin and Chu could not prevail against it. Such is a worthy man’s capacity to stand firm!

I have heard that Jin drew upon the enduring strength of its successive hegemonies; no northern state was stronger. Zheng lay to its south, anxiously complying with its wishes, fearful of falling behind. When Gongsun Xia attacked Chen and Zichan presented the spoils of victory, Jin questioned Zheng’s invasion of a small state and challenged his wearing military dress. It intended to put Zheng in the wrong and attack it. Had no one been able to answer, could Zheng have escaped? Fortunately, Zichan carried out his mission, tracing the great virtue of Chengzhou and proclaiming the great beneficence of his former ruler. With “abandoning our close kin,” he enumerated Chen’s offenses; with “many Jiao, several royal domains” [?], he refuted Jin’s arguments; with “each resuming his former duties,” he reaffirmed the king’s command. His bearing was upright and his language reasonable. Even Shi Zhuangbo’s eloquence could find no further scope, while “to attack those who follow what is right is inauspicious” brought Zhao Wen to a realization. Otherwise, Jin, with its territory extending a thousand li, might have demanded military levies and provoked a calamity whose consequences could not be measured. How could it possibly have been willing to accept Zheng’s presentation of victory?

As for Chu, it was a barbarian state that had usurped the royal title, yet no southern state was stronger. Zheng lay close to its northern border, fearful and scarcely able to keep pace with its commands. Before the meeting at Guo, when Ziwei was planning his marriage, his proposed entry into the guest quarters and his plan to bring a large company to fetch the bride were intended to take Zheng by surprise and seize its state. Had no one been able to resist, would Zheng not have been in peril? Fortunately, Zichan supplied the words for a reply, explaining the small state’s innocence and holding the great state responsible for maintaining peace. “We request that a cleared ceremonial ground be prepared outside” checked his arrogance; “harboring a heart bent on calamity” exposed his treachery; “resisting and contravening your lord’s command” [?] reinforced the warning to him. His principles were correct and his words stern; although…

title: 嘉靖三十七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
以伯州犁之對卒不能勝而垂櫜請入竟成伍
舉之議矣不然帶甲十萬之楚乗虚而入國且
莫之保也而况於豐氏之祧哉是則不患有晋
楚之強而患無子産以禦其強不患於鄭國之
弱而患無子産以振其弱強為善而已矣而仲
之見脅忽之出奔所以貶於春秋也抑晋以重
幣而失陳僑也惑之已見譏於子産圍懷禍心
而即會執戈前矣方見誚於子皮己則不縮而
欲以無道加諸人也胡可得哉宜乎鄭之得伸
===
其氣也噫楚無足責也晋國列卿不能繼魏絳
智罃之策而于虢之會楚遂先歃人才之有關
於國家也不可見哉

以伯州犁之對，卒不能勝，而垂櫜請入，竟成伍舉之議矣。不然，帶甲十萬之楚乗虚而入，國且莫之保也，而况於豐氏之祧哉？是則不患有晋楚之強，而患無子産以禦其強；不患於鄭國之弱，而患無子産以振其弱。強為善而已矣。而仲之見脅、忽之出奔，所以貶於春秋也。抑晋以重幣而失陳，「僑也惑之」，已見譏於子産；圍懷禍心，而即會執戈前矣，方見誚於子皮。己則不縮，而欲以無道加諸人也，胡可得哉？宜乎鄭之得伸其氣也！噫！楚無足責也，晋國列卿不能繼魏絳、智罃之策，而于虢之會，楚遂先歃。人才之有關於國家也，不可見哉？
秋九月，齊侯、宋公、江人、黄人盟於貫。〔僖公〕二年。
同考試官教諭楊批：胡傳中「慮周義著」，意實相成，非可分言也。士子率多分言之，而意反不達。獨此篇融會傳意，能發齊桓制楚之心，且語意莊雅，識見透徹，非優于經
translation_en:
…even with Bo Zhouli’s reply, they ultimately could not prevail. They therefore lowered their bow cases and requested admission, finally carrying out Wu Ju’s proposal. Otherwise, Chu, with its hundred thousand armored troops, would have taken advantage of the opening to enter; even the state could not have been preserved, much less the ancestral temple of the Feng lineage. Thus the worry was not that Jin and Chu were powerful, but that there might be no Zichan to resist their power; not that Zheng was weak, but that there might be no Zichan to revive it from weakness. One need only strive to do what is good. Zhong’s being coerced and Hu’s flight into exile were the reasons they were censured in the Spring and Autumn Annals. Moreover, Jin’s losing Chen through its demands for lavish gifts had already drawn Zichan’s criticism: “I, Qiao, am perplexed by this.” Wei harbored malicious intentions, yet approached the meeting bearing a dagger-axe [?], and was then rebuked by Zipi. If one is oneself in the wrong, how can one hope to impose lawless demands upon others? It was fitting that Zheng could assert its spirit!
Alas! Chu scarcely merits reproach. But Jin’s high ministers could not carry on the policies of Wei Jiang and Zhi Ying, and at the meeting at Guo, Chu consequently took precedence in sipping the covenant blood. Does this not show how greatly men of talent matter to a state?
In autumn, in the ninth month, the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, and representatives of Jiang and Huang concluded a covenant at Guan. Second year of Duke Xi.
Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor: In Hu’s Commentary, the ideas expressed by “deliberation was thorough and righteousness manifest” in fact complement one another and cannot be discussed separately. Examination candidates generally discuss them separately, thereby failing to convey the meaning. This essay alone integrates the commentary’s meaning and brings out Duke Huan of Qi’s intention to check Chu. Moreover, its language and thought are dignified and refined, and its understanding penetrating. Unless one excels in the study of the Classics…

title: 嘉靖三十七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
學者不能也宜錄以式
考試官侍讀高批得聖人予齊桓意
考試官學士董批有斷制
伯主交遠以制外春秋特予之也此貫之盟桓
之工於謀楚也春秋爲世道計則安得而不予
乎且盟春秋之所惡也貫之盟桓服江黃也而
予之者何夫正天下之分存乎義義不著則分
幾乎斁矣成天下之事存乎慮慮不周則義幾
乎息矣想桓之意以爲中國不可不尊也而荆
===
楚侵強則憑陵日至且有左衽之憂矣惡在其
能尊乎強夷不可不攘也而江黃爲與則氣勢
方張且有右臂之援矣惡在其可攘乎故一匡
之志本以荆楚爲謀而萬全之舉先以江黃爲
計於是乎冠裳畢會而講信以結其心牲歃爲
盟而脩睦以聯其好不惟離之於楚而且使之
附於齊蓋以彼之與與我而其威乃可振也不
徒使附於齊而且用以制乎楚蓋以我之敵敵
彼而其勢乃可撓也運籌壇坫之上而制勝江

考試官侍讀高批：得聖人予齊桓意。
考試官學士董批：有斷制。
伯主交遠以制外，春秋特予之也。此貫之盟，桓之工於謀楚也。春秋爲世道計，則安得而不予乎？且盟，春秋之所惡也。貫之盟，桓服江黃也，而予之者何？夫正天下之分存乎義，義不著，則分幾乎斁矣；成天下之事存乎慮，慮不周，則義幾乎息矣。想桓之意，以爲中國不可不尊也，而荆楚侵強，則憑陵日至，且有左衽之憂矣，惡在其能尊乎？強夷不可不攘也，而江黃爲與，則氣勢方張，且有右臂之援矣，惡在其可攘乎？故一匡之志，本以荆楚爲謀，而萬全之舉，先以江黃爲計。於是乎冠裳畢會，而講信以結其心；牲歃爲盟，而脩睦以聯其好。不惟離之於楚，而且使之附於齊，蓋以彼之與與我，而其威乃可振也；不徒使附於齊，而且用以制乎楚，蓋以我之敵敵彼，而其勢乃可撓也。運籌壇坫之上，而制勝江
translation_en:
…learning could not accomplish this. It should be recorded as a model.
Examiner Gao, Reader-in-waiting, comments: “This captures the sage’s intention in approving Duke Huan of Qi.”
Examiner Dong, Academician, comments: “It shows decisive judgment.”
When a hegemon establishes relations with distant states to restrain external powers, the Spring and Autumn Annals accords him special approval. This covenant at Guan shows Duke Huan’s skill in planning against Chu. Since the Spring and Autumn Annals takes account of the moral order of the world, how could it withhold approval? Yet covenants are something the Spring and Autumn Annals condemns. The covenant at Guan brought Jiang and Huang into submission to Duke Huan; why, then, does it receive approval? Rectifying the distinctions of rank throughout the realm depends upon righteousness. If righteousness is not made manifest, those distinctions come close to collapse. Accomplishing the affairs of the realm depends upon forethought. If forethought is not comprehensive, righteousness comes close to extinction.
We may imagine Duke Huan reasoning that the central states must be upheld in honor. Yet, with Jing-Chu encroaching and growing powerful, its depredations increased daily, and there was even cause to fear that people would wear their robes fastened on the left, in the manner of the foreign peoples. How, then, could the central states be upheld? The powerful foreign peoples must be repelled. Yet, with Jiang and Huang as their allies, their strength and influence were expanding, and they had support like a right arm. How, then, could they be repelled?
Thus his resolve to set the realm aright was fundamentally directed against Jing-Chu, but his measures to ensure complete success began with plans concerning Jiang and Huang. Accordingly, those wearing ceremonial caps and robes all assembled, and pledges of good faith won their hearts. They made a covenant by tasting the blood of sacrificial victims, cultivating concord to bind their friendship. He not only detached them from Chu but also brought them into allegiance to Qi: by making the other side’s allies his own, he could thereby assert his authority. He not only brought them into allegiance to Qi but also used them to restrain Chu: by turning his own enemies against the other side, he could thereby undermine its power. He devised his strategy at the ceremonial altar and secured victory on the banks of the Jiang…

title: 嘉靖三十七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
漢之濱雖陽穀之會未舉所以糾合而撻伐之
者固已有成筭矣震疊蠻夷之心而發舒華夏
之氣雖陘亭之師未次所以聲罪而壓服之者
固已有全圖矣是其慮之周也而義因以著義
之著也而慮之周者益足多焉君子謂是役也
庶幾乎武王之誓遠及八國之人紹美於大公
之烈光昭四至之命者也故諸侯皆在而於內
獨言宋公於外獨言江黃者若曰宋其大者也
舉其大而小可知也江黃其遠者也舉其遠而
===
近可知也非以深與之而何哉抑桓之謀仲教
之也惜也遠齊近楚仲預憂之而桓遽忘之也
卒見滅於楚而不救夫楚之甘心於彼固也彼
慕吾義而来而吾乃卒忍心焉則何哉噫方其
盛也楚之與國吾能有之及其衰也吾之與國
楚能滅之夷夏消長之幾寔決於此此桓之所
以為桓而聖門不道者也
禮記
天子以德為車以樂為御

punctuated:
漢之濱，雖陽穀之會未舉，所以糾合而撻伐之者，固已有成筭矣。震疊蠻夷之心，而發舒華夏之氣，雖陘亭之師未次，所以聲罪而壓服之者，固已有全圖矣。是其慮之周也，而義因以著；義之著也，而慮之周者益足多焉。君子謂是役也，庶幾乎武王之誓遠及八國之人，紹美於大公之烈，光昭四至之命者也。故諸侯皆在，而於內獨言宋公，於外獨言江黃者，若曰：「宋其大者也，舉其大而小可知也；江黃其遠者也，舉其遠而近可知也。」非以深與之而何哉？抑桓之謀，仲教之也。惜也，遠齊近楚，仲預憂之，而桓遽忘之也。卒見滅於楚而不救。夫楚之甘心於彼，固也；彼慕吾義而来，而吾乃卒忍心焉，則何哉？噫！方其盛也，楚之與國，吾能有之；及其衰也，吾之與國，楚能滅之。夷夏消長之幾，寔決於此。此桓之所以為桓，而聖門不道者也。

禮記

天子以德為車，以樂為御。
translation_en:
…on the banks of the Han. Although the meeting at Yanggu had not yet been held, a settled plan already existed for rallying the allies and launching a punitive campaign against Chu. To strike terror into the hearts of the Man and Yi peoples and give free rein to the spirit of Huaxia: although the army had not yet encamped at Xingting, a complete plan already existed for proclaiming Chu’s offenses and compelling its submission. Such was the thoroughness of his deliberations, through which his righteousness became manifest. With his righteousness manifest, the thoroughness of his deliberations became all the more praiseworthy. The gentleman would say that this undertaking came close to King Wu’s oath, which reached even the people of eight states, carrying forward the glory of Taigong’s achievements and making illustrious the mandate extending to the four boundaries.

Thus, although all the regional lords were present, the record names only the Duke of Song among the inner states and only Jiang and Huang among the outer states. It is as though it said: “Song is the great one among them; by mentioning the great, the small may be understood. Jiang and Huang are the distant ones; by mentioning the distant, the near may be understood.” What could this be but profound approval?

Yet Duke Huan’s strategy was taught to him by Guan Zhong. Alas! Jiang and Huang were far from Qi and close to Chu: Guan Zhong worried about this beforehand, but Duke Huan soon forgot it. In the end they were destroyed by Chu, and he did not rescue them. That Chu should vent its wrath upon them was to be expected. But they had come to us in admiration of our righteousness; how could we ultimately harden our hearts against them? Alas! At the height of his power, we could win over Chu’s allies; when his power declined, Chu could destroy ours. The turning point in the waxing and waning of the Yi peoples and the Xia states was determined precisely here. This is what made Duke Huan the ruler he was, and why the disciples of Confucius did not speak of him.

Record of Rites

The Son of Heaven takes virtue as his carriage and music as his charioteer.

text:
同考試官教諭顏批說理精徹措詞莊雅
末復徵以中庸之言尤爲有見佳作佳作
考試官侍讀高批明整可誦
考試官學士董批天子之德樂不同而欲切
之車御尤難敷衍惟此作識其大故錄之
大君動無不正而用無不和此順之達也盖德
者出治之本而樂也者和此者也由於德而成
於樂則大君之順歸焉耳昔先王之治人情也
===
本修已之功極成物之效而家而國既無不順
者矣况天子者天下之主而達順之原也所以
自盡其道者何如哉彼行必有車也天子則以
德爲車焉夫德非可以車言也惟其利用出入
而無適不然則德固猶車也已今也建中於上
而萬化妙其權輿體道於身而百行循其軌轍
自其心之正者而時措焉以正百官以正萬民
皆其運用者也自其性之盡者而率由焉以盡
人之性以盡物之性皆其推行者也盖雖無庸

Comment by Examiner Gao, Reader-in-waiting: “Clear and well ordered; worthy of recitation.”

The great sovereign is correct in every action and harmonious in every exercise of his powers: this is the full realization of accord. Virtue is the foundation from which good government proceeds, while music brings it into harmony. Originating in virtue and perfected through music, the great sovereign’s accord thus finds its fulfillment. In ancient times, when the former kings regulated human feelings, they took the work of self-cultivation as their foundation and brought to its utmost the efficacy of bringing other beings to fulfillment. Within both family and state, nothing failed to accord. How much more is this true of the Son of Heaven, the lord of all under Heaven and the source from which accord reaches everywhere! How, then, does he fully carry out his Way? When one travels, one must have a chariot; the Son of Heaven takes virtue as his chariot. Virtue cannot, strictly speaking, be spoken of as a chariot. Yet because it facilitates his going out and coming in, and does so wherever he goes, virtue is indeed like a chariot. He establishes the mean above, and the myriad transformations find their wondrous beginnings therein; he embodies the Way in his person, and his hundred forms of conduct follow its tracks. From the rectitude of his own heart, he acts as circumstances require, rectifying the hundred officials and the myriad people: all these are exercises of his virtue. From the full realization of his own nature, he follows its course, bringing the nature of other people and the nature of things to full realization: all these extend the practice of his virtue. Thus, although there is no need …

title: 嘉靖三十七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
於輪轅之飾寔有相與周流而無間者矣謂德
之非車也可乎哉車必有御也天子則以樂爲
御焉夫樂非可以御言也惟其用以和德而無
行不與則樂固猶御也已今也歡欣浹洽而統
馭之道弘優柔平中而操縱之機熟以心之和
爲氣之和凡所運用自適緩急之宜也以氣之
和爲形之和惟所推行咸中肅雍之度也盖雖
無假於和鸞之美寔有相與周旋而不舍者矣
謂樂之非御也可乎哉夫以德爲車則其化也
===
不行而自至以樂爲御則其治也無爲而自成
此固順之所由達而天下之所以肥者歟抑於
是而知中庸之言徵也夫中和致而天地位萬
物育聖德修而天下肥四靈至其義一也聖神
之功化豈誣也哉然中庸言修己而教在其中
禮運言治人而必原諸修己可見聖德大業初
非二事而帝王之道誠本於心者也
方以類聚物以羣分則性命不同矣

方以類聚物以羣分則性命不同矣
punctuated:
於輪轅之飾，寔有相與周流而無間者矣。謂德之非車也，可乎哉？車必有御也，天子則以樂爲御焉。夫樂非可以御言也，惟其用以和德而無行不與，則樂固猶御也已。今也歡欣浹洽，而統馭之道弘；優柔平中，而操縱之機熟。以心之和爲氣之和，凡所運用，自適緩急之宜也；以氣之和爲形之和，惟所推行，咸中肅雍之度也。盖雖無假於和鸞之美，寔有相與周旋而不舍者矣。謂樂之非御也，可乎哉？夫以德爲車，則其化也不行而自至；以樂爲御，則其治也無爲而自成。此固順之所由達，而天下之所以肥者歟！抑於是而知《中庸》之言徵也。夫中和致而天地位、萬物育，聖德修而天下肥、四靈至，其義一也。聖神之功化，豈誣也哉？然《中庸》言修己，而教在其中；《禮運》言治人，而必原諸修己。可見聖德大業，初非二事，而帝王之道，誠本於心者也。

方以類聚，物以羣分，則性命不同矣。
translation_en:
…the adornment of wheels and shafts, there is indeed something that accompanies it in ceaseless circulation. Can one say that virtue is not a carriage? A carriage must have a charioteer; the Son of Heaven takes music as his charioteer. Music cannot literally be called a charioteer. Yet because it serves to harmonize virtue and participates in every action, music is indeed like a charioteer. Now, joy and delight permeate all, and the way of governing becomes broad; ease, gentleness, balance, and centeredness prevail, and the art of directing and regulating becomes practiced. Through harmony of the heart, harmony of the vital energies is achieved, so that every exercise of power naturally attains the proper measure of slowness and urgency. Through harmony of the vital energies, harmony of bodily form is achieved, so that everything put into effect accords with the measure of reverence and concord. Though there is no need to borrow the beauty of the carriage bells, there is indeed something that accompanies every movement without ceasing. Can one say that music is not a charioteer? With virtue as his carriage, his transforming influence arrives of itself without traveling; with music as his charioteer, his governance succeeds of itself without deliberate action. Surely this is how harmonious obedience spreads and how all under Heaven flourish!

From this, moreover, we know that the words of the Doctrine of the Mean are borne out. When equilibrium and harmony are fully realized, Heaven and Earth take their proper places and the myriad things are nurtured. When sagely virtue is cultivated, all under Heaven flourish and the four numinous creatures appear. The meaning is the same. How could the transformative achievements of the sage's spiritual potency be unfounded? Yet the Doctrine of the Mean speaks of cultivating oneself, with the teaching of others included within it; the “Evolution of Rites” speaks of governing others, but necessarily traces this back to cultivating oneself. Thus we can see that sagely virtue and great undertakings were never two separate matters, and that the Way of emperors and kings truly has its root in the heart.

Activities gather according to kind, and things divide according to their group; thus their natures and allotted destinies differ.

title: 嘉靖三十七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭顏批性命不同處作者皆知
爲聖人制禮之本但體脈不明詞多浮泛此篇理致深融
且文有繩墨一字不苟真傑士也敬服敬服
考試官侍讀高批純實
考試官學士董批義精詞達
知人事之異其宜當知天理之異其分蓋天理
在人自有不同之分也則夫人事之異宜也謂
非本於是者哉樂記君子謂夫人徒知禮之制
於聖人而不知其本於造化是豈獨君臣貴賤
===
大小之間爲然哉夫人倫有五固各有其方也
然倫之乃可以爲倫豈容泛焉而無當乎於是
乎比而合之而五典則有五惇以天合者聯之
以恩以人合者協之以義各從其類非可以假
借爲也經禮有五固各有其物也然經之乃可
以爲經豈容混焉而無別乎於是乎理而分之
而五禮則有五庸禮之常者以處事之常禮之
變者以處事之變各歸其分非可以參互爲也
此聖人之所以制禮也然豈創自聖人者哉誠

知人事之異其宜，當知天理之異其分。蓋天理在人，自有不同之分也，則夫人事之異宜也，謂非本於是者哉？《樂記》君子謂：夫人徒知禮之制於聖人，而不知其本於造化，是豈獨君臣貴賤大小之間爲然哉？夫人倫有五，固各有其方也。然倫之乃可以爲倫，豈容泛焉而無當乎？於是乎比而合之，而五典則有五惇。以天合者聯之以恩，以人合者協之以義，各從其類，非可以假借爲也。經禮有五，固各有其物也。然經之乃可以爲經，豈容混焉而無別乎？於是乎理而分之，而五禮則有五庸。禮之常者以處事之常，禮之變者以處事之變，各歸其分，非可以參互爲也。此聖人之所以制禮也，然豈創自聖人者哉？誠
translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner Yan, Instructor: All the writers recognize that differences in nature and heavenly endowment form the basis upon which the sages instituted ritual. Yet their compositions lack a clear structure and continuity, and their language is often superficial and vague. This essay’s reasoning is profound and thoroughly integrated; its writing also observes proper standards, with not a single carelessly chosen word. Truly an outstanding scholar! My admiration and respect, my admiration and respect!
Comment by Examiner Gao, Reader-in-Waiting: Pure and substantial.
Comment by Examiner Dong, Academician: Precise in meaning and lucid in expression.
To understand that human affairs differ in what is appropriate to them, one must understand that heavenly principle makes different allotments. For heavenly principle as embodied in human beings inherently assigns them different portions. Could one say that the different requirements of human affairs are not grounded in this? The gentleman in the Record of Music says: People know only that ritual was instituted by the sages, but do not know that it is rooted in the creative transformations of Heaven and Earth. Could this hold only for the distinctions between ruler and minister, noble and lowly, great and small? There are five human relationships, each certainly possessing its own proper way. Yet if these relationships are truly to constitute ordered relationships, how could they be left vague, without anything fitting to them? Thus they are brought together according to their affinities, and the five cardinal relationships each receive their own means of being strengthened. Those joined by Heaven are bound by affection; those joined through human agency are harmonized through righteousness. Each follows its own kind; these bonds cannot be fashioned by borrowing indiscriminately from others. There are five categories of canonical rites, each certainly having its own objects. Yet if these rites are truly to constitute enduring norms, how could they be confused without distinction? Thus they are ordered and differentiated, and the five categories of rites each have their own established application. Regular rites address ordinary affairs; adapted rites address exceptional affairs. Each belongs to its own allotted sphere; they cannot be performed by indiscriminately mixing one with another. This is how the sages instituted ritual. Yet could it have originated with the sages themselves? Indeed …

title: 嘉靖三十七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
以我之得於天者曰性而天之賦於我者曰命
禮之所由生也是雖出於一原然天有顯道厥
類彰焉而變化之初即具夫各正之體是雖統
於一心然民之秉彝各有則焉而渾然之理自
涵夫燦然之條尊之不可使爲卑猶夫卑之不
可使爲尊孰是與定乃分限之自有者也五典
而五惇自天叙之而已然矣厚之不可使爲薄
猶夫薄之不可使爲厚孰是與辨乃情理之自
至者也五禮而五庸自天秩之而已然矣是知
===
性命自有分聚之殊而方物本乎性命之理則
夫聖人之於禮也夫豈無因而强作者哉大抵
斯章之言皆取諸易而義則有不同者蓋易明
天道故以造化之妙顯於卦爻禮明人事故以
制度之宜原諸造化要之卦爻之中莫非人倫
之理其所象者固即其所法者也觀此則禮之
本諸天地也爲益信而不聞性與天道信乎不
足以有制也
第貳塲

第貳場
punctuated:
以我之得於天者曰性，而天之賦於我者曰命，禮之所由生也。是雖出於一原，然天有顯道，厥類彰焉，而變化之初即具夫各正之體；是雖統於一心，然民之秉彝各有則焉，而渾然之理自涵夫燦然之條。尊之不可使爲卑，猶夫卑之不可使爲尊，孰是與定？乃分限之自有者也。五典而五惇，自天叙之而已然矣。厚之不可使爲薄，猶夫薄之不可使爲厚，孰是與辨？乃情理之自至者也。五禮而五庸，自天秩之而已然矣。是知性命自有分聚之殊，而方物本乎性命之理，則夫聖人之於禮也，夫豈無因而强作者哉？大抵斯章之言皆取諸易，而義則有不同者。蓋易明天道，故以造化之妙顯於卦爻；禮明人事，故以制度之宜原諸造化。要之，卦爻之中莫非人倫之理，其所象者固即其所法者也。觀此，則禮之本諸天地也爲益信，而不聞性與天道，信乎不足以有制也。

第貳塲
translation_en:
…for what we receive from Heaven is called our nature, while what Heaven bestows upon us is called its mandate: these are the source from which ritual arises. Although these issue from a single source, Heaven has its manifest Way, whose categories are clearly displayed; from the very beginning of transformation, the constitution by which each thing attains its proper place is already present. Although these are united in a single mind, the constant qualities held by the people each have their norms; the undivided principle inherently contains its distinct and brilliant articulations. The honored cannot be made lowly, just as the lowly cannot be made honored. Who has determined this? These distinctions and limits exist of themselves. That the five cardinal relationships each receive their due cultivation has been so ever since Heaven ordered them. Those to be treated generously cannot be treated sparingly, just as those to be treated sparingly cannot be treated generously. Who has distinguished these? Such distinctions arise naturally from human feeling and principle. That the five rites each have their constant practice has been so ever since Heaven ranked them. Thus we know that human nature and Heaven’s mandate inherently contain distinctions of separation and association, and that distinguishing things rests upon the principles of nature and mandate. Could the sages, then, have arbitrarily devised ritual without any foundation?

Generally, the words of this chapter are all drawn from the Book of Changes, yet their meaning differs. The Book of Changes elucidates the Way of Heaven, and therefore displays the subtleties of creation and transformation in its hexagrams and their lines. The Book of Rites elucidates human affairs, and therefore traces the fitting arrangements of institutions to creation and transformation. Ultimately, everything within the hexagrams and their lines embodies the principles of human relationships: what the Changes represents is precisely what the Rites takes as its model. Viewed in this light, it becomes still more certain that ritual is rooted in Heaven and Earth. Indeed, without understanding human nature and the Way of Heaven, one cannot establish institutions.

Discourse
The Sages Have Rendered Service to All under Heaven for Myriad Generations

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Instructor: The enduring and vast achievements of the sages stand alongside Heaven and Earth and are difficult to express in words. This composition probes the deepest mysteries of principle and elucidates them thoroughly and fully. Its author has a refined understanding of the sages and worthies. I admire it! I admire it!

Comment by Associate Examiner Sun, School Director: This essay elucidates the Way of the sages, exploring it repeatedly over several thousand words, yet leaving implications that cannot be exhausted. It is like the sword Ganjiang drawn from its case, its edge irresistible, or Bian He's jade once polished, its radiance impossible to restrain. It rightly merits first place among those recommended from the metropolitan region. It is recorded here to serve as a model.

Comment by Associate Examiner Xing, metropolitan graduate (jinshi): The sages embody this Way and can therefore devise institutions suited to their times to serve as models for posterity. This composition offers precise elucidation and deeply grounded argument; it weaves together Heaven and humanity and arrays its ideas like the constellations. Reading it is like living in the age of the Five Emperors, with its expansive, harmonious spirit. An excellent composition, deserving to be recorded first.

Comment by Examiner Gao, Reader-in-waiting: This discourse traces matters from source to outcome and knows when to draw together and when to open out. It is like Wang Liang's charioteering: racing all day without departing from the proper measure. An extraordinary talent! An extraordinary talent!

Comment by Examiner Dong, Academician: To discuss the achievements of the sages is like portraying Heaven and Earth. If an author merely embellishes them with ornate language, he falls far short. This essay has a broad and lofty spirit and particularly deserves first place among those recommended.

translation_en:
…and preserves it: this is called the heart-mind. The heart-mind is what all people throughout the world and across the ages alike possess. The sage puts it into operation through this heart-mind: this is called the Way. The Way is what all people throughout the world and across the ages alike follow. Yet although they possess it in common, they cannot fully realize it themselves; although they follow it in common, they cannot attain it for themselves. The sage therefore establishes institutions and standards for them, enabling those unable to realize it fully to do so, and those unable to attain it to do so. This is how the sage makes it accessible throughout the world and across the ages. In making it accessible, the sage merely proceeds from what all share; he adds nothing of his own. People, too, attain what they share in common and lead one another to rest content in the sage’s institutions and standards, without being compelled. All this is the embodiment of the Way.

The Song Confucian scholar Hu says that the Five Emperors rendered service to the world and to all subsequent ages. Can he be someone with whom one may discuss the Way? What, then, is the Way? It is the unifying order of Heaven and Earth, the regular course of sun and moon, the sequence of the four seasons, the guiding framework of human relationships, the hidden essence of civilization, the convergence of canonical norms, what is fitting in every particular of things, and the source of all affairs and transformations. It is the principle that gives life to human beings, which they possess in its integrated entirety as their heart-mind. Now, human beings’ luminous intelligence and awareness penetrate all things because they possess this heart-mind. Throughout the Four Seas, local ways differ; in the five regions, customs differ. Yet people communicate through voice and vital energy because they possess this heart-mind. They respond to one another across distant places and resonate with one another across widely separated ages; the incipient impulses within them communicate because they possess this heart-mind. …their uniting and possessing it within themselves. Yet although people unite and possess it within themselves, they cannot fully realize it all; hence in some respects they are obstructed, and in others they attain understanding. Those who practice without discerning and act without understanding are ordinary people: they are obstructed. Those who seek understanding and discernment through practice and action are learners: they seek to attain understanding. Those who understand and discern but sometimes fall short are gentlemen: they have attained understanding, but not fully. Ordinary people need not be discussed, and there is no time here to discuss learners. If gentlemen wish to apply their still incomplete understanding to government, their minds must contain areas of obscurity that they have not penetrated; this is called leaving something outside. Their minds must contain divisions that they have not brought into unity; this is called having interruptions. To seek the Way, which leaves nothing outside, with a mind that leaves something outside is impossible. To seek the Way, which never ceases, with a mind subject to interruptions is impossible. Thus one may understand small matters yet be obstructed in great ones; understand this yet be obstructed in that; understand the present yet be obstructed in what comes afterward. Sages embrace both small and great, unite this and that, and comprehend past and present, attaining understanding throughout. This is the embodiment of the Way. Thus Fuxi began it, Shennong continued it, and Huangdi, Yao, and Shun continued it in turn. This is what the five sages transmitted to one another as they upheld the one Way.
Thus, when Heaven and Earth were not yet settled and no one had grasped their governing unity, they made a revolving canopy [?], recorded the celestial paths and lodges, and examined the jade astronomical mechanism and sighting tube; the measures of Heaven were thereby set right. That the sages grasped this governing unity, so that Heaven and Earth necessarily became settled, is the embodiment of the Way. …waxing and waning, so that shadows could be measured; they determined the surplus requiring intercalation and duly established the year’s beginning [?], so that the seasons could be announced. That the sages grasped the governing order of these things, and the sun, moon, and four seasons consequently could not but follow their proper courses: this is the substance of the Way.

When human relationships were not yet clear and no one had grasped their guiding principles, and patterned civilization had not yet been made manifest and no one had grasped its mysteries, the sages ordered the five cardinal relationships and disseminated the five teachings, and human relationships became clear. They modeled the trigrams on the River Chart and created writing to replace knotted cords, and patterned civilization became manifest. That the sages grasped these guiding principles and mysteries, and human relationships consequently could not but become clear and patterned civilization could not but become manifest: this is the substance of the Way.

When institutions and standards were not yet comprehensive and no one had grasped how they fitted together, the sages standardized measures and weights, giving people something to observe; set forth models and patterns, giving them something to follow; and established rites and music, providing the means for their transformation. Thus the institutions and standards were laid out in detail. When the particulars of material life were not yet fully provided for and their appropriate arrangements had not been attained, the sages taught people to use plows and plowshares to till and sow, enabling them to feed themselves; made dwellings and implements for them, enabling them to settle; and aided them with medicine, enabling them to obtain relief. Thus the benefits of material equipment became complete. That the sages grasped how these things fitted together and what was appropriate to them, and institutions and standards consequently could not but become comprehensive and the particulars of material life could not but be fully provided for: this is the substance of the Way.

As for the source of all affairs and transformations, through which full provision is made for all people, all things, and all matters of governance under Heaven, the sages shaped and assisted them, establishing regulations and models for them, putting these into effect in their own time and transmitting them to later generations, leaving nothing out. 非樂于有所創而亦非樂于無所爲也樂于有
所創則心勞樂于無所爲則心寂聖人寂然不
動感而遂通凡以心之無所與而純乎道之體
也心無所與故有以通天下萬世之心純乎道
之體故天下萬世皆取足于吾道而聖人非有
所加也人亦非有所强也吾嘗驗夫人心之偶
得而不涉之以事也則其中必有藹然和矣其
===
外必有油然順矣其觀之天地萬物必有廓然
與我同者矣此聖人所以通天下萬世之本也
是心之得也非獨聖人有之凡民亦有之凡民
有之是心體之本同也其失也非獨凡民有之
君子亦有之君子有之是心體之難盡也聖人
以其所難盡者盡之而以其所同具者爲之制
爲之法使之率而由之以各得其心故當時不
能違而後世不能易非不能違與易其心之本
同而道之無以復加也今夫公輸子天下之善

…the sage dares not lag behind it. Before the time has come, what is done cannot be called unduly simple: the Way requires that one not act prematurely. Once the time has come, what is done cannot be called unduly elaborate: the Way requires that one not lag behind. The sage takes pleasure neither in introducing innovations nor in doing nothing. Delight in innovation wearies the heart; delight in doing nothing leaves the heart inactive. The sage is quiescent and unmoving, yet when stimulated responds with complete understanding. This is entirely because his heart has no private involvement and accords purely with the substance of the Way. Because his heart has no private involvement, he can commune with the hearts of all people throughout the world and across the ages. Because he accords purely with the substance of the Way, all people throughout the world and across the ages find full sufficiency in our Way. The sage adds nothing to it, nor are others subjected to any constraint.

I have observed that when a person's heart happens to attain this state, without affairs intruding upon it, there is necessarily a gentle harmony within and a spontaneous ease without. In contemplating Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things, one necessarily feels an expansive sense that they are one with oneself. This is the foundation upon which the sage communes with all people throughout the world and across the ages. Such attainment of the heart belongs not only to sages; ordinary people also possess it. That ordinary people possess it shows that the substance of the heart is fundamentally the same in all. Nor is its loss confined to ordinary people; gentlemen also experience it. That gentlemen experience it shows how difficult it is to realize fully the substance of the heart.

The sage fully realizes what is so difficult to realize and, on the basis of what all alike possess, establishes institutions and standards for them. He causes them to follow these, so that each may attain his own heart. Thus his contemporaries cannot depart from them, and later generations cannot alter them. title: 嘉靖三十七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
工也天下不能皆工而知公輸子之善以其規
矩無以復加也養由基天下之善射也天下不
能皆射而知養由基之善以其彀率無以復加
也聖人之于道猶公輸之規矩而養由之彀率
也故聖人之始也能以天下爲一人萬世爲一
息者非意之也道之體也而其旣也天下安之
萬世仰之亦道之體也故自聖人之定天地也
天下萬世相生相養于覆載之中以爲聖人之
功而聖人不自知也自聖人之曆象日月四時
===
也天下萬世順其晝夜寒暑之序以爲聖人之
功而聖人不自知也自聖人之别倫理而開人
文也天下萬世得其禮義之分而窺其精微之
蘊以爲聖人之功而聖人不自知也自聖人之
立典則而辨物曲也天下萬世循其爲政之方
而沿其日用之利以爲聖人之功而聖人不自
知也自聖人啓萬事萬化之原而天下萬世人
得其性物得其軌精粗巨細無一而不得其常
由之則治違之則亂以爲聖人之功而聖人不

…a skilled craftsman. Not everyone in the world can be a craftsman, yet all recognize the excellence of Gongshu Zi, because his compass and square admit of no improvement. Yang Youji was the world's master archer. Not everyone in the world can shoot, yet all recognize Yang Youji's excellence, because his standards for drawing the bow admit of no improvement. The sage's relation to the Way is like Gongshu's compass and square and Yang Youji's standards for drawing the bow. Thus, at the outset, the sage can regard all under Heaven as one person and ten thousand generations as a single breath. This is no mere imagining: it is the essential reality of the Way. And afterward, when all under Heaven find repose in it and ten thousand generations look up to it, this too is the essential reality of the Way.

Thus, ever since the sages established Heaven and Earth in their proper order, people throughout the world and across ten thousand generations have brought one another into life and sustained one another beneath Heaven's covering and upon Earth's support. They regard this as the sages' achievement, yet the sages themselves are unaware of it. Ever since the sages calculated and observed the sun, moon, and four seasons, people throughout the world and across ten thousand generations have followed the succession of day and night, cold and heat. They regard this as the sages' achievement, yet the sages themselves are unaware of it. Ever since the sages distinguished human relationships and inaugurated human culture, people throughout the world and across ten thousand generations have attained their proper distinctions in ritual and righteousness and gained insight into their subtle depths. They regard this as the sages' achievement, yet the sages themselves are unaware of it. Ever since the sages established canonical rules and distinguished the particulars of things, people throughout the world and across ten thousand generations have followed their methods of government and enjoyed the benefits they provided for daily life. They regard this as the sages' achievement, yet the sages themselves are unaware of it. Ever since the sages opened up the source of all affairs and transformations, people throughout the world and across ten thousand generations have realized their proper natures, and things have attained their proper courses. Whether subtle or coarse, great or small, nothing fails to attain its constant norm. Following it brings order; departing from it brings disorder. They regard this as the sages' achievement, yet the sages do not…

title: 嘉靖三十七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
自知也故無聖人則天地毀矣天地不毀則聖
人之功常在也無聖人則日月四時紊矣日月
四時不紊則聖人之功常在也無聖人則人倫
不明文明不著典則不立物曲不備萬事萬化
不行矣天下萬世而可以無是數者則已其不
可無則聖人之功常在也是皆道之本無可外
本無可息而聖人無所與也故曰道之體也抑
吾觀堯舜聖人之獨盛者也其相授受曰允執
厥中吾知道之體在是也而伏羲以下吾不得
===
而觀焉吾以為三聖人之道無可得而見也及
吾讀易而觀易卦實始于伏羲孔子之賛易則
曰黃帝堯舜取諸乾坤而神農取諸益乃知數
聖人皆深于易者而易之一書實所以明中也
夫中者道之體也故吾以為聖人之有功於天
下萬世本于道而已非臆說也

punctuated:
自知也。故無聖人則天地毀矣，天地不毀則聖人之功常在也；無聖人則日月四時紊矣，日月四時不紊則聖人之功常在也；無聖人則人倫不明，文明不著，典則不立，物曲不備，萬事萬化不行矣。天下萬世而可以無是數者則已，其不可無，則聖人之功常在也。是皆道之本無可外，本無可息，而聖人無所與也，故曰道之體也。抑吾觀堯舜，聖人之獨盛者也，其相授受曰：「允執厥中。」吾知道之體在是也，而伏羲以下，吾不得而觀焉。吾以為三聖人之道無可得而見也。及吾讀《易》而觀，《易》卦實始于伏羲，孔子之賛《易》則曰黃帝、堯、舜取諸乾坤，而神農取諸益，乃知數聖人皆深于《易》者，而《易》之一書實所以明中也。夫中者，道之體也。故吾以為聖人之有功於天下萬世，本于道而已，非臆說也。

translation_en:
…yet the sages themselves are unaware of it. Thus, without the sages, Heaven and Earth would collapse; so long as Heaven and Earth do not collapse, the sages’ achievement endures. Without the sages, the sun, moon, and four seasons would fall into disorder; so long as these do not fall into disorder, the sages’ achievement endures. Without the sages, human relationships would not be clarified, civilization would not become manifest, norms would not be established, the particulars of things would not be fully provided for, and the myriad affairs and transformations would not proceed. If the world throughout all ages could dispense with these things, there would be nothing more to say; but since it cannot, the sages’ achievement endures. All this is because the Way inherently leaves nothing outside itself and never ceases; the sages do not deliberately bring it about. Hence it is called the substance of the Way.

Now, I consider Yao and Shun to be the most illustrious among the sages. In transmitting rule from one to the other, they said, “Sincerely hold fast to the Mean.” I know that the substance of the Way lies here, but I have been unable to observe it in Fuxi and those who followed him. I had thought that the Way of the Three Sages could no longer be discerned. Yet when I read and examined the Book of Changes, I found that its hexagrams indeed originated with Fuxi. In his elucidation of the Changes, Confucius says that Huangdi, Yao, and Shun took their models from Qian and Kun, while Shennong took his from Yi, or Increase. Only then did I understand that these sages were all deeply versed in the Changes, and that the Book of Changes in fact serves to illuminate the Mean. The Mean is the substance of the Way. Thus my contention that the sages’ achievement for the world throughout all ages is rooted solely in the Way is no mere conjecture.

translation_en:
…Righteous duty finds expression in remedying deficiencies, with correcting the troubles of the age especially urgent. I have often heard of the tradition of frank assent and dissent, and imagine those distant days of enlightened rulers and worthy ministers. Gao Yao expounded his counsels to Yu of Xia, stressing the difficulty of benevolence and discernment [?]; Fu Yue presented his instructions to the Shang king, urging him to take the perceptive and wise as his model. Thoroughly understanding the three categories of appointment was Ji Dan’s admonition concerning the employment of men; displaying the might of the six armies was the Duke of Shao’s exhortation to preserve Heaven’s Mandate. For when sages govern the world, even in security they do not consider themselves secure; thus loyal ministers, in their devotion to their sovereign, seek ever greater preparedness even when all is already provided for.
Your servant has long received abundant imperial favor, yet has found no means to render the service of a dog or horse. I have always cherished an unadorned loyalty and count myself fortunate to bear the admonitory responsibility once entrusted to blind court musicians. I have indeed examined the men of antiquity and investigated the reasons for their success and failure; from this I have turned to contemporary affairs, seeking the foundations of good government. Taking counsel with my own heart and lips, I have considered a hundred concerns. What I seem to have grasped of the essentials amounts to no more than three points. These thoughts have accumulated within me, difficult to convey, while my earnest concern never ceases. Though, like the man of Qi, I worry excessively and presumptuously fear that Heaven may fall, still, finding my humble celery exceedingly sweet, I cannot abandon the wish to offer it to Your Majesty.
For I have reverently encountered in Your Majesty one who continues Yao’s divine sagacity and carries forward Yu’s frugality and diligence. You regard freedom from hoarding as wealth, and freedom from killing as authority: gracious as the warmth of spring sunshine. translation_en:
…extends even to men living in obscurity; in accepting remonstrance, You gather counsel even from the humblest sources. You have gloriously renewed Your mighty undertaking, bringing forty years of splendid harmony, and magnificently established a grand foundation, extending the blessings of peace through countless ages. Yet, because tranquil prosperity has endured so long, those charged with enforcing the laws often lapse into following established routines. As indolence gradually becomes habitual, those administering government come to prize indulgence. This prevents the imperial influence from spreading freely; how could it be said that Your Majesty’s beneficence has not been broadly extended?

Nevertheless, tightening and relaxing require different methods, and there are proper occasions for exercising control or granting latitude. It is from the Son of Heaven alone that rites, music, and punitive expeditions proceed; within the August Norm, firmness, mildness, and uprightness complement one another. Benevolence must therefore employ discernment to prevent obstruction and concealment, while discernment must also be joined with martial resolve to support bold decisions. These must, moreover, be balanced and mutually sustaining, without partiality; only then can they operate together without conflict.

As for the widespread neglect of duty among officials, it all arises from confusion between nominal standing and actual performance. And when military preparedness steadily declines, what use is an imposing display of sound and spectacle? Select Your officials, make rewards trustworthy and punishments certain, and there may then be men who follow the proper order and faithfully discharge their duties [?]. Inspect actual conditions, eliminate superfluous personnel, and seek excellence; then there will be dependable means of resisting aggression and repelling attacks. These are all ways of establishing good government and securing the state. Are they merely remedies for imbalance and abuses? They have been appropriate since antiquity and are still more urgently needed today.

Your servant has therefore arranged these matters under three headings and appended a few words, comparing and cross-checking what I have previously learned. punctuated: 言。雖管測井窺，莫識乾坤之廣大，顧纖塵涓露，少裨海嶽之崇深。仰瀆重瞳，備觀乙夜，竊比孟軻之敬，非道不陳於前；願爲君陳之良，有謀乃順於外。伏望轉圜量闊，止輦心虛，帝德罔愆，加之意而高明光大；王猶允塞，見諸事以深切著明。百工釐，庶績熙，不假彌文之飾；萬邦寧，四夷順，遹觀道化之成。則國家大曆將與天地無疆，而臣子寸心不随草木同朽。臣無任瞻天仰聖、激切屏營之至，謹以三劄随表上進以聞。
translation_en: …words. Though, peering through a tube or from a well, I cannot comprehend the vastness of Heaven and Earth, I hope that these motes of dust and drops of dew may contribute a little to the loftiness of the mountains and the depth of the seas. I venture to trouble Your Majesty’s august gaze, submitting this for your reading during the second watch of the night. I humbly seek to emulate Meng Ke’s reverence, presenting before you nothing that accords not with the Way; I wish to emulate Jun Chen’s excellence, carrying your counsels into effect beyond the court. I prostrate myself and hope that Your Majesty will show the breadth of mind to turn as readily as a revolving sphere and the humility to halt your imperial carriage to hear counsel. May your imperial virtue remain without fault and, through further attention, become lofty, luminous, and expansive; may your royal counsels be truly complete and, embodied in affairs, become profound, pertinent, manifest, and clear. May all officials discharge their duties and all undertakings flourish, without recourse to elaborate literary embellishment; may the myriad states be at peace and the peoples of the four quarters submit, so that we may behold the accomplishment of transformation through the Way. Then the state’s allotted span will be as boundless as Heaven and Earth, and this servant’s humble devotion will not perish together with the grasses and trees. Gazing toward Heaven and looking up to Your sagely Majesty, your servant is overcome with fervent emotion, awe, and trepidation. I respectfully submit these three notes together with this memorial for Your Majesty’s hearing.

Third Session
Five Policy Questions
Brief Introduction

Associate Examiner Wu, Instructor (jiaoyu), comments: Our Emperor’s way of serving Heaven is rooted in reverence. The means by which he reaches the august heavens and brings blessings in profusion are profoundly subtle and difficult to express. This composition alone succeeds in celebrating and extolling them, revealing the sincerity of its author’s loyalty and devotion.

Associate Examiner Lin, Instructor (xuezheng), comments: Our Emperor reverently performs the sacrifices to Heaven; their ceremonial forms and the governance associated with them shine like the sun and stars. All the candidates can expound upon and praise these. But few can elucidate the essential meaning of serving Heaven: how it accords with that of the ancient emperors and kings and forms the foundation for manifestly receiving abundant blessings. This composition expounds and celebrates it fully; loyalty and devotion overflow beyond the words, revealing what its author has cultivated within himself.

title: 嘉靖三十七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
皇上敬
天一念所以卓邁百王者正以
獨得其精動靜語默無非
昭格之所也子能歷陳之其有古人歌頌
君德之風者乎人臣之道宜如此故錄焉
執事以帝王事天之道下策承學淺陋不
足以奉明問雖然
大聖人之化則涵濡久矣請述所聞于古者而
後對揚
今日之盛可乎愚嘗觀事天之文自羲農以
上無所復見蓋杜佑稱黃帝作合宮以事
上帝開明庭以祀天神合宮明庭之制雖
不可考大槩事天之文自黃帝始矣及舜
受命于堯而有肆類之禮有禋徧之儀則
其文益著及三代至周而益以備焉是故
陶匏之器藁秸之藉疏布之冪樿杓之薦
貴其文之有質也邸鎮之圭五采之繅八
變之樂龍章之斿貴其文之飾也帝王之

punctuated:
皇上敬天一念，所以卓邁百王者，正以獨得其精，動靜語默，無非昭格之所也。子能歷陳之，其有古人歌頌君德之風者乎？人臣之道宜如此，故錄焉。
執事以帝王事天之道下策，承學淺陋，不足以奉明問。雖然，大聖人之化則涵濡久矣。請述所聞于古者，而後對揚今日之盛，可乎？愚嘗觀事天之文，自羲農以上，無所復見。蓋杜佑稱黃帝作合宮以事上帝，開明庭以祀天神。合宮、明庭之制雖不可考，大槩事天之文自黃帝始矣。及舜受命于堯，而有肆類之禮，有禋徧之儀，則其文益著。及三代，至周而益以備焉。是故，陶匏之器、藁秸之藉、疏布之冪、樿杓之薦，貴其文之有質也；邸鎮之圭、五采之繅、八變之樂、龍章之斿，貴其文之飾也。帝王之
translation_en:
…His Majesty’s single-minded reverence for Heaven surpasses that of the hundred kings precisely because he alone has grasped its essence. In movement and stillness, in speech and silence, everything he does reaches Heaven with luminous sincerity. You have set this forth point by point: do you not possess something of the spirit in which the ancients sang praises of their rulers’ virtue? Such is the proper way for a subject to act; hence this essay has been selected for inclusion.
You, the officials presiding, have set a policy question on how emperors and kings served Heaven. My learning is shallow and inadequate to answer your discerning inquiry. Nevertheless, I have long been steeped in the transforming influence of our great sage ruler. May I recount what I have learned of antiquity and then respond by extolling the glory of the present day? I have examined the ceremonial forms for serving Heaven, but for the time of Fuxi and Shennong and earlier, no further evidence can be found. Du You states that Huangdi built the Hegong, the Palace of Union, to serve the Supreme Lord, and opened the Mingting, the Bright Court, to sacrifice to the celestial spirits. Although the arrangements of the Hegong and Mingting cannot be ascertained, broadly speaking, the ceremonial forms for serving Heaven began with Huangdi. When Shun received the mandate from Yao, there were the lei sacrifice to the Supreme Lord and the ceremonies of pure offerings made universally to the spirits; thus these forms became more manifest. Through the Three Dynasties, they became still more complete under the Zhou. Thus, vessels of earthenware and gourds, mats of straw, coverings of coarse cloth, and the presentation of plain wooden ladles expressed the value placed on substance within ceremonial form. Jade gui tablets with bases of the zhen type, silk pads in five colors, music in eight successive variations, and banner streamers bearing dragon designs expressed the value placed on ceremonial embellishment. As for emperors and kings…

title: 嘉靖三十七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
于文也可謂盡心爾矣夫文者帝王所以
綢繆其敬者也而政者帝王所以經緯其
文者也吾觀黃帝推筴迎日以正天統使
時有可紀焉建天地神祇物類之官民是
以有忠信神是以有明德民神得業而事
可舉焉盖黃帝之政非徒以其文而已也
至堯舜則始命羲和分命叔仲脩曆象正
璣衡而歲成焉殷四仲之序定四時之法
釐百工熈庶績而民治焉盖堯舜之政亦
===
非徒以其文而已也至周則有司會以協

…in their attention to ritual forms, may truly be said to have devoted their utmost care. Ritual forms are the means by which emperors and kings give sustained expression to their reverence; government is the means by which they order and organize those forms. I observe that Huangdi calculated with counting rods and determined the arrival of the sun to rectify the celestial succession, so that time could be reckoned. He established offices responsible for heaven, earth, spirits, and the various categories of beings. Thus the people possessed loyalty and trustworthiness, and the spirits manifested luminous virtue; people and spirits each fulfilled their proper functions, and undertakings could be carried out. Huangdi’s government, then, did not consist merely in ritual forms.

With Yao and Shun, Xi and He were first commissioned, and separate charges were assigned to the younger and middle brothers. They perfected calendrical observations and adjusted the celestial instruments, thereby completing the reckoning of the year. They correctly ordered the middle months of the four seasons and established the rules governing those seasons; they regulated the hundred offices and brought their many undertakings to fruition, so that the people were well governed. The government of Yao and Shun, too, did not consist merely in ritual forms.

Under the Zhou, there was an Accounts Manager to harmonize the five calendrical measures [?], an Astrologer to distinguish the five celestial phenomena, an Astronomer to oversee the eight stars [?], and a Minister of Education to measure the four seasonal sun-shadows. Their establishment of offices was exceedingly thorough. The five calendrical measures served to establish the Supreme Standard; the five celestial phenomena, to disclose ominous portents; the eight stars, to distinguish and order activities; and the four seasonal sun-shadows, to determine the origins of seasonal vital energies. These arrangements bore most directly upon moral transformation and good order. Zhou government, too, did not consist merely in ritual forms.

Thus, when emperors and kings have ritual forms as standards for their conduct, they must also have government as an all-encompassing system of regulation. title: 嘉靖三十七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
存高明之天心以是敬而運之謂之天德
故發之則以成文施之則以成政是皆敬
之不容已者也吾嘗讀傳記稱黃帝命史
甲作戶牖巾几諸銘以箴切左右而巾几
所云毋𢠵德毋犯義者其詞有獨至焉其
斯黃帝之所為敬者乎若堯舜則典謨所
載著多矣而其大者曰欽曰慎曰恭君德
盛矣而猶曰克艱至治極矣而猶曰儆戒
其斯堯舜之所為敬者乎若周則又有可
===
識者矣以文王之昭事而猶不顯亦臨無
斁亦保以武王之執競而猶拜洪範作肅
之言受丹書之旨而成王則儀刑二后夙
夜基命日監在茲尤不遑暇焉其斯周文
武成王之所為敬者乎夫敬者道之體也
天者道之原也帝王以敬會道則道在我
以道會天則天在我故黃帝之神化宜民
與天下無為者天也其聖智創物以為天
下利者亦天也堯舜之文思安安垂衣而

translation_en: …preserve the lofty and luminous mind of Heaven. To put it into operation through this reverence is called heavenly virtue. Thus, when expressed, it produces cultural forms; when applied, it produces government. These are all irrepressible manifestations of reverence. I have read in transmitted accounts that Huangdi commanded the scribe Jia to compose inscriptions for doors, windows, cloths, and tables, to admonish those around him. Among these, the words on the cloths and tables, “Do not neglect virtue [?]; do not transgress righteousness,” are particularly incisive. Was this not how Huangdi practiced reverence? As for Yao and Shun, much is recorded in the Canons and Counsels of the Book of Documents. Its principal terms are “reverence,” “caution,” and “respect.” Although their sovereign virtue was abundant, it still speaks of “recognizing the difficulty”; although perfect government had reached its height, it still speaks of “vigilance and caution.” Was this not how Yao and Shun practiced reverence? With the Zhou, there is still more to observe. King Cheng took the two former kings as his models, establishing Heaven’s mandate morning and night and daily keeping his attention fixed upon it, allowing himself especially little leisure. Was this not how Kings Wen, Wu, and Cheng of Zhou practiced reverence? Reverence is the embodiment of the Way; Heaven is the source of the Way. When emperors and kings unite with the Way through reverence, the Way resides in them; when they unite with Heaven through the Way, Heaven resides in them. Thus, Huangdi’s wondrous transformation of the people for their well-being, and his governing all under Heaven through nonaction, were Heaven at work. title: 嘉靖三十七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
治者天也其兢兢業業一日萬幾者亦天
也周之不識不知順帝之則者天也其是
伐是肆以耆爾功者亦天也至此則帝王
與天張弛與天出入神融意會聲應氣求
此天下之至精也如是而文興焉則天帝
可質而其文亦精矣如是而政舉焉則天
運可求而政亦精矣如是而天不愛道地
不愛寶休徵畢至貞符咸集而帝王蒙天
之福盛矣然帝王往矣千載而下其
===
卓越帝王者不在我
皇上乎蓋
皇上正
南郊之專祀上
皇天之泰號建
玄極以祭于內搆
玄穹以祭于外禮有合也則雖帝王未之有可
得而起也禮有未合也則雖
當世所已行可得而改也是我

…bringing order was Heaven; their reverent vigilance in attending to the myriad affairs of each day was also Heaven. The Zhou rulers’ acting without conscious knowledge or calculation, following the Lord on High’s pattern, was Heaven; their attacking and striking to bring their achievement to completion was also Heaven. At this point, sovereigns tighten and relax in accord with Heaven, advance and withdraw in accord with Heaven. Their spirits blend and their intentions meet; corresponding sounds respond to one another, and kindred vital forces seek one another. This is the utmost refinement in all under Heaven. When cultural forms flourish in this way, the Lord of Heaven may be called upon to bear witness, and those forms too are refined. When government is conducted in this way, Heaven’s workings may be discerned, and government too is refined. Thus Heaven does not withhold its Way, nor Earth its treasures; auspicious signs arrive in full, and favorable portents all gather. Abundant indeed are the blessings that sovereigns receive from Heaven! Yet those sovereigns have passed away. A thousand years later, is it not our Emperor who surpasses them?
For our Emperor has rectified the exclusive worship of Heaven at the Southern Suburb, bestowed the exalted designation “August Heaven,” built Xuanji for sacrifices within, and constructed Xuanqiong for sacrifices without. title: 嘉靖三十七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
皇上于事
天之文卓然有
振古之見矣至于星辰一失其度即軫之
聖懷雨暘一違其期即形之
宸慮風沙一異其常即切之
淵念旱潦一過其節即動之
皇言所以防其未然杜其有漸者不必重黎之
後疇人之守也則是我

===
天之政卓然有

敬一箴而觀所謂
匪敬弗聚匪一弗純斯言也其即唐虞之秘
旨乎又至于

傳乎及至于祀

translation_en:
…His Majesty, in the ceremonial forms of serving Heaven, has displayed an outstanding vision unequaled since antiquity. Whenever the stars depart from their proper courses, his sagely heart is troubled; whenever rain or sunshine fails to arrive at its appointed time, his imperial concern becomes manifest; whenever wind and sand deviate from their usual pattern, his profound thoughts turn urgently to them; whenever drought or flooding exceeds its seasonal bounds, he gives voice to his concern in imperial pronouncements. In forestalling these things before they occur and checking their incipient development, he need not depend upon the descendants of Chong and Li or the custodianship of hereditary astronomical specialists. Thus, in his governance in service to Heaven, our Majesty has displayed an outstanding vision unequaled since antiquity.
When I, in my ignorance, turn to the Admonition on Reverence and Unity (Jingyi zhen) and consider its words, “Without reverence, there is no gathering together; without unity, there is no purity,” are these not the profound teachings of Yao and Shun? Again, when I turn to the Explanation of the Four Admonitions (Si zhen shuo) and consider its words, “Look and listen in accordance with ritual propriety; speak and act in accordance with ritual propriety,” are these not the authentic transmission of Confucius and Yan Hui? title: 嘉靖三十七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
親授面諭以賜羣臣有曰
君人者父母
天地而爲之子必若父子焉有曰知所尊以尊
尊焉凡一言一動以至於慶賞刑罰則不敢
私一己之欲知所親以親親焉凡出入語默
以及于民物則不敢作纖毫之惡與夫過不
及之患乃盡事
天如父之道斯言也其帝王所未有而不可以
復加者乎盖以事
===
父之道事
天則通爲一氣帝王之敬所以爲精也以
慶賞刑威則合爲一體精之至矣以
出入語默則無所不用其精
天與道一道與
天一而敬爲渾化矣故其因前代之法而考古
證今以
折衷百王是
精之所爲也立

punctuated: 親授面諭，以賜羣臣，有曰：「君人者父母天地而爲之子，必若父子焉。」有曰：「知所尊以尊尊焉，凡一言一動，以至於慶賞刑罰，則不敢私一己之欲；知所親以親親焉，凡出入語默，以及于民物，則不敢作纖毫之惡，與夫過不及之患，乃盡事天如父之道。」斯言也，其帝王所未有而不可以復加者乎？盖以事父之道事天，則通爲一氣，帝王之敬所以爲精也。以慶賞刑威，則合爲一體，精之至矣；以出入語默，則無所不用其精。天與道一，道與天一，而敬爲渾化矣。故其因前代之法，而考古證今，以折衷百王，是精之所爲也。立
translation_en:
…he personally bestowed these teachings upon his assembled ministers and instructed them face to face, saying: “The ruler of men takes Heaven and Earth as his parents and becomes their son; their relationship must be like that of father and son.” He also said: “Knowing whom to revere, one honors those worthy of honor. In every word and action, extending to celebrations, rewards, punishments, and penalties, one dares not indulge one’s own selfish desires. Knowing whom to hold dear, one cherishes one’s kin. In going out and coming in, in speech and silence, and in dealings with the people and all things, one dares not commit the slightest evil or incur the fault of excess or deficiency. Only then does one fully realize the Way of serving Heaven as one’s father.” Are these not words that no emperor or king has previously uttered, and to which nothing further can be added?
When one serves Heaven by the Way of serving one’s father, all is joined in a single vital energy: this is what makes the reverence of emperors and kings pure. In celebrations, rewards, and the awe of punishment, all is united as one body: this is purity at its utmost. In going out and coming in, in speech and silence, there is nowhere that this purity is not applied. Heaven is one with the Way, and the Way is one with Heaven; reverence thus becomes wholly integrated and transformative. Hence, his following the institutions of former dynasties, examining antiquity to verify the present, and weighing the practices of the hundred kings—all this is the work of purity. Establishing…

punctuated: 一王之制，而垂統作則，以駕越萬世，亦精之所爲也。率其文，由其政，循其典則，以相貫通，是精之所爲也。文自我出，政自我立，操其機緘，以爲運用，亦精之所爲也。故帝王之事天，猶爲有方；有方則滯。而皇上宮居宴處，儼然周壇，則無方所而無非天矣。帝王之事天，猶爲有時；有時則間。而皇上早暮晝夜，肅然對越，則無時日而無非天矣。帝王之事天，猶爲有迹；有迹則粗。而皇上動靜游衍，凛然鑒臨，則不拘于迹而無非天矣。故皇上之寧神淵默，而體道會元，是即天之於穆也。皇上之總攬乾綱，而臨機英斷，是即天之剛健也。
translation_en:
…the institutions of a sovereign, transmitting a line of succession and establishing standards that transcend ten thousand generations: this too is the work of purity of concentration. Following inherited cultural forms, proceeding according to established governance, and observing canonical standards so that they interconnect: this is the work of purity of concentration. Bringing forth cultural forms oneself, establishing governance oneself, and grasping the controlling mechanisms to put them into operation: this too is the work of purity of concentration.

Thus, emperors and kings still served Heaven within particular places; confinement to place entails obstruction. Yet Your Majesty, dwelling in the palace or resting at ease, maintains the same solemn bearing as at the Zhou altar [?]. There is consequently no restriction of place: everywhere is Heaven. Emperors and kings still served Heaven at particular times; restriction to time entails interruption. Yet Your Majesty, morning and evening, day and night, reverently faces Heaven. There is consequently no restriction of time or day: always there is Heaven. Emperors and kings still served Heaven through outward forms; outward forms entail coarseness. Yet Your Majesty, in movement and stillness, in recreation and repose, remains awesomely mindful of Heaven’s scrutiny and presence. There is consequently no confinement to outward forms: all is Heaven.

Thus, Your Majesty’s calming the spirit in profound silence, embodying the Way and comprehending the primal source, is precisely Heaven’s profound solemnity. Your Majesty’s grasping the sovereign reins and making discerning, decisive judgments as circumstances arise is precisely Heaven’s strength and vigor.

神焉是其

===

皇上之察見四海而洞照萬微，朝廷有大議、遇大事，諸司百僚方惶惑無措，而疏入立報，無不稱神焉。是其明即天之日月也。

皇上之軫念閭閻，矜惻民隱，稍有歲儉而賑使四出，詔令所至，無不懽呼鼓舞，以飽易饑，以生回槁者。是其恩即天之雨露也。

皇上之鼓舞不測，內晰奸逆，外戡寇暴，江之南、冀之北，羽檄一馳，而廟謨勝算運于几席，赫赫嘽嘽，震動萬里。是其威即天之雷霆也。然猶
translation_en:
His Majesty surveys all within the four seas and penetrates every subtle detail. When the court faces weighty deliberations or momentous affairs, while the offices and their officials are still bewildered and at a loss, memorials receive an immediate response upon submission; all acclaim this as divine. His illumination is thus the sun and moon of Heaven.

His Majesty bears the common people in his thoughts and feels compassion for their hidden sufferings. At the slightest scarcity in the harvest, relief commissioners go forth in every direction. Wherever his edicts reach, all cheer and rejoice: hunger gives way to satiety, and those withered by privation are restored to life. His beneficence is thus the rain and dew of Heaven.

His Majesty stirs people to action in unfathomable ways. Within, he discerns treachery and rebellion; without, he subdues bandits and violent aggressors. South of the Yangzi and north of Ji, once urgent military dispatches speed forth, strategies of certain victory are devised at his desk in the court. Resplendent and mighty, they shake ten thousand li. His majesty is thus the thunder of Heaven. Yet still…

title: 嘉靖三十七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
神運而不已
心勞而不懈天下已安而
慮存邊隅志關武備未嘗一日忘也萬事已
理而
躬親機務深究化原未嘗一日忘也蓋合黃
帝堯舜周文武成王之敬而兼總其全者
是即
天之流行而不息也故
三光昭明百神擁護
===
太階平六符正甘露降靈澤濡是
蒼蓋之効禎也固
天之福也黃河清醴泉出紫芝朱草之生
獻無虛日嘉禾瑞穀之產史不歇書玄鶴降
白鹿來
瑞應奇兆不可枚舉是
黃輿之協順也亦
天之福也而要其極則皆
皇上事

punctuated: 神運而不已，心勞而不懈。天下已安，而慮存邊隅，志關武備，未嘗一日忘也；萬事已理，而躬親機務，深究化原，未嘗一日忘也。蓋合黃帝、堯、舜、周文、武、成王之敬，而兼總其全者，是即天之流行而不息也。故三光昭明，百神擁護，太階平，六符正，甘露降，靈澤濡，是蒼蓋之効禎也，固天之福也。黃河清，醴泉出，紫芝朱草之生，獻無虛日；嘉禾瑞穀之產，史不歇書；玄鶴降，白鹿來，瑞應奇兆，不可枚舉，是黃輿之協順也，亦天之福也。而要其極，則皆皇上事
translation_en:
…His spirit works without ceasing, and his mind labors without slackening. Though all under Heaven is already at peace, his thoughts remain with the frontier regions and his attention with military preparedness: not for a single day does he forget them. Though the myriad affairs are already well ordered, he personally attends to the crucial business of government and probes deeply into the sources of moral transformation: not for a single day does he forget these. He unites the reverence of the Yellow Emperor, Yao, Shun, and Kings Wen, Wu, and Cheng of Zhou, embracing it in its entirety. This is Heaven’s ceaseless movement itself.

Thus the three luminaries shine brightly, and the hundred spirits offer protection. The Three Steps constellation is balanced, its six stars correctly aligned; sweet dew descends, and numinous moisture spreads. These are the auspicious signs manifested by the azure canopy of the sky—surely blessings from Heaven. The Yellow River runs clear, and springs of sweet water emerge. Purple numinous mushrooms and crimson plants appear, with not a day passing without their presentation at court. Auspicious grain and propitious cereals grow, and the historians never cease recording them. Black cranes descend, and white deer come. These auspicious responses and wondrous omens are too numerous to enumerate. They show the harmonious compliance of the yellow earth and are likewise blessings from Heaven. Yet, traced to their ultimate source, they are all His Majesty’s service to …

title: 嘉靖三十七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
天之明效大驗而
至敬之符也夫
皇上之福海內之人能頌之矣
皇上之文與政學士大夫能言之矣而
皇上之會其精者則雖在
庭之臣有不能知而愚何敢與焉雖然無所
不覆者
天之大也昭昭者
天之可見者也愚之所言盖亦昭昭者耳惟執
===
事進而教之
第二問
同考試官教諭顏批我
朝設官斟酌古今制莫善焉後因文例日增故不免增設我

punctuated:
天之明效大驗，而至敬之符也。夫皇上之福，海內之人能頌之矣；皇上之文與政，學士大夫能言之矣。而皇上之會其精者，則雖在庭之臣有不能知，而愚何敢與焉？雖然，無所不覆者，天之大也；昭昭者，天之可見者也。愚之所言，盖亦昭昭者耳。惟執事進而教之。
第二問
同考試官教諭顏批：我朝設官，斟酌古今，制莫善焉。後因文例日增，故不免增設。我皇上時裁罷之，真聖人之獨見。子能詳言其意，而又推究多事之源，欲臣工務實求當，以仰稱上意，不惟識見超越，而忠懇尤可嘉也。敬服，敬服！
考試官侍讀髙批：多事因以多官，所見良是。所
translation_en:
…are clear proofs and great confirmations of his service to Heaven, and tokens of his utmost reverence. All within the seas can extol His Majesty’s blessings; scholars and officials can speak of His Majesty’s cultural achievements and governance. Yet even ministers at court may fail to understand how His Majesty brings together their essential principles; how could an ignorant man such as I venture to discuss this? Nevertheless, Heaven’s greatness lies in leaving nothing uncovered, while its manifest aspects are what we can see. What I have said concerns, perhaps, only these manifest aspects. I ask you, sir, to guide and instruct me further.
Second Question
Comment by Associate Examiner Yan, Instructor: In establishing offices, our dynasty weighed ancient and modern practice; no system could be better. Later, as documentary precedents increased daily, additional offices inevitably had to be established. Our Emperor has from time to time reduced or abolished them: this truly displays a sage’s unique insight. You explain his intention fully and also investigate the source of the proliferation of business. You wish officials to attend to substantive matters and seek appropriate solutions, thereby fulfilling His Majesty’s wishes. Not only is your discernment outstanding, but your loyal sincerity is especially commendable. I admire you, I admire you!
Comment by Examiner Gao, Expositor-in-Waiting: The proliferation of business leads to a proliferation of officials: your view is indeed correct. …

title: 嘉靖三十七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
以務省事者又鑿鑿可行經生而能知時務若此乎
考試官學士董批少魯人能言矣要知由于省
事夫去蠹在本節流在源務實求當此其要指也子能詳陳之
其有志世用者與佳士佳士
君之使臣將以乂民而非為備也臣之事
君將以建事而非為文也惟無裨於事而
為空文故無裨於民而為徒備也而又益
官以治則備乃所以擾而文乃所以蠹譬
之以醯祛蚋以肉驅鼠去之愈疾其至愈
===
疾何則以致之之道去之也若去之而知
所以去則幾矣夫上古之治莫唐虞成周
若也其風朴其政醇其庶績咸熙其萬物
咸若乃其設官也教養工虞禮樂刑曆分
命而不以攝也百揆四岳州牧侯伯並建
而不以兼也公孤論燮卿牧率倡相聯若
此其密也設參傳伍置輔陳殷相維若此
其周也則亦若甚詳矣乃稽其數則惟曰
唐虞官百而已周官三百六十而已周視

以務省事者，又鑿鑿可行。經生而能知時務若此乎！
考試官學士董批：少魯人能言矣，要知由于省事。夫去蠹在本，節流在源，務實求當，此其要指也。子能詳陳之，其有志世用者與！佳士！佳士！
君之使臣，將以乂民，而非為備也；臣之事君，將以建事，而非為文也。惟無裨於事而為空文，故無裨於民而為徒備也。而又益官以治，則備乃所以擾，而文乃所以蠹。譬之以醯祛蚋，以肉驅鼠，去之愈疾，其至愈疾。何則？以致之之道去之也。若去之而知所以去，則幾矣。夫上古之治，莫唐虞成周若也。其風朴，其政醇，其庶績咸熙，其萬物咸若。乃其設官也，教養、工虞、禮樂、刑曆，分命而不以攝也；百揆、四岳、州牧、侯伯，並建而不以兼也。公孤論燮，卿牧率倡，相聯若此其密也；設參傳伍，置輔陳殷，相維若此其周也。則亦若甚詳矣。乃稽其數，則惟曰唐虞官百而已，周官三百六十而已。周視
translation_en:
…the means proposed for reducing administrative business are, moreover, firmly grounded and practicable. Can a student of the Classics understand contemporary affairs so well?
Examiner Dong, Academician, comments: “The young man of Lu can speak [?]. The essential point is to understand that this depends on reducing administrative business. To eliminate harm, address its roots; to restrict the flow, address its source. Pursue substance and seek what is appropriate: this is the central principle. You have set it out fully. Surely you aspire to practical service in the world! An excellent scholar! An excellent scholar!”
A ruler employs ministers to bring order to the people, not merely to fill out an establishment; ministers serve their ruler to accomplish affairs, not merely to maintain formalities. Precisely because they contribute nothing to affairs and amount to empty formalities, they contribute nothing to the people and merely fill places. If still more officials are added to administer matters, the establishment itself becomes a source of disturbance, and formalities become a source of harm. This is like using vinegar to repel gnats or meat to drive away rats: the more urgently one drives them away, the more swiftly they arrive. Why? Because one uses the means of attracting them to drive them away. If, in seeking to remove them, one understood the proper means of removal, one would be close to success.
Among the governments of high antiquity, none equaled those of Tang and Yu or the established Zhou dynasty. Their customs were simple, their governance pure, their many undertakings all flourished, and all things found their proper order. In establishing offices, they assigned separate responsibilities for instruction and sustenance, crafts and natural resources, rites and music, punishments and calendrical reckoning, without having officials act provisionally in other posts. The General Regulator, the Four Mountains, Regional Governors, and the lords of the various ranks were established together, without concurrent appointments. The Three Dukes and Three Solitary Dignitaries deliberated and harmonized; ministers and regional governors led and guided. So closely were they linked together. They established groups of three and five, appointed auxiliaries, and arrayed a multitude of officers [?]. So comprehensive was their mutual support. The arrangements would thus appear exceedingly elaborate. Yet when one examines their numbers, one finds only that Tang and Yu had a hundred officials, and Zhou three hundred and sixty. Compared with…

title: 嘉靖三十七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
唐虞雖稍增廣然有不必備者又多兼者
又冢宰歲終詔廢置司士歲登下損益之
數則猶有廢而損者非多也且勿論上世
即如漢高帝時海內不混一乎然以三公
統九卿以丞相史分刺郡國决獄或責廷
尉衞屯或至詔罷官之省可知也後乃加
設漸多司農之外復有水衡中尉之外復
有校尉諸如羽林期門綉衣直指之類盖
視昔幾倍之焉而治則不逮又如唐太宗
===
時海內不治平乎然以六部繼三省以九
寺繼六部臺有御史獨司糾察監有八監
互以相繼官之省可知也後乃加設漸多
水陸有使矣而租庸又置使度支有使矣
而鹽鐵又置使諸如木炭青苗户口羣牧
之類盖視昔幾倍之焉而治則不逮夫官
皆前寡而後多治皆前隆而後替此其故
何也則前之事務减而後之事務增减者
益務所以减而增者益務所以增故也夫

設漸多司農之外復有水衡中尉之外復
有校尉諸如羽林期門綉衣直指之類蓋
視昔幾倍之焉而治則不逮又如唐太宗
===
時海内不治平乎然以六部繼三省以九
寺繼六部臺有御史獨司糾察監有八監
互以相繼官之省可知也後乃加設漸多
水陸有使矣而租庸又置使度支有使矣
而鹽鐵又置使諸如木炭青苗户口羣牧
之類蓋視昔幾倍之焉而治則不逮夫官
皆前寡而後多治皆前隆而後替此其故
何也則前之事務減而後之事務增減者
益務所以減而增者益務所以增故也夫
punctuated:
唐虞雖稍增廣，然有不必備者，又多兼者。又冢宰歲終詔廢置，司士歲登下損益之數，則猶有廢而損者，非多也。且勿論上世，即如漢高帝時，海內不混一乎？然以三公統九卿，以丞相史分刺郡國，决獄或責廷尉，衞屯或至詔罷，官之省可知也。後乃加設漸多，司農之外復有水衡，中尉之外復有校尉，諸如羽林、期門、綉衣直指之類，盖視昔幾倍之焉，而治則不逮。又如唐太宗時，海內不治平乎？然以六部繼三省，以九寺繼六部，臺有御史獨司糾察，監有八監互以相繼，官之省可知也。後乃加設漸多，水陸有使矣，而租庸又置使；度支有使矣，而鹽鐵又置使。諸如木炭、青苗、户口、羣牧之類，盖視昔幾倍之焉，而治則不逮。
夫官皆前寡而後多，治皆前隆而後替，此其故何也？則前之事務减，而後之事務增，减者益務所以减，而增者益務所以增故也。夫
translation_en:
…although the number had increased somewhat over that of Tang and Yu, there were offices that need not all be filled, and many were held concurrently. Moreover, at year's end the Grand Steward advised on dismissals and appointments, while the Director of Officials annually recorded the numbers promoted and demoted, reduced and increased. Thus there were still abolitions and reductions, rather than a proliferation of offices.
Leaving remote antiquity aside, was not the realm unified under Emperor Gao of Han? Yet the Three Dukes supervised the Nine Chamberlains, and clerks of the Chancellor were separately dispatched to inspect the commanderies and kingdoms. Adjudicating cases might be entrusted to the Chamberlain for Law Enforcement, and guard garrisons might even be abolished by imperial decree. From this one can see how few offices there were. Later, additional offices gradually multiplied. Besides the Chamberlain for the National Treasury, there was also a Chief Commandant of Waterways and Parks; besides the Commandant of the Capital, there were also commandants. Such establishments as the Feathered Forest Guards, the Attendant Guards, and the Embroidered-Robe Investigating Emissaries brought their number to several times that of earlier days, yet government did not match its former quality.
Again, was not the realm peaceful and well governed under Emperor Taizong of Tang? Yet the Six Ministries followed the Three Departments, and the Nine Courts followed the Six Ministries. In the Censorate, censors alone handled scrutiny and impeachment; among the directorates, eight directorates complemented one another [?]. From this one can see how few offices there were. Later, additional offices gradually multiplied. There were already commissioners for water and land transport, yet commissioners for grain taxes and labor-service commutation were also established. There were already commissioners for expenditure planning, yet commissioners for salt and iron were also established. Such offices as those for charcoal, green-sprout levies, household registration, and the state herds brought their number to several times that of earlier days, yet government did not match its former quality.
In each case, offices were few at first and numerous later, while government flourished at first and subsequently declined. Why was this? Because administrative business diminished earlier and increased later: those who reduced it devoted themselves ever more to the means of reducing it, while those who increased it devoted themselves ever more to the means of increasing it. title: 嘉靖三十七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
人恒自淳而趨僞物恒自朴而趨華禮恒
自簡而趨繁俗恒自厚而趨薄匪直近代
爲然即周視唐虞亦有間矣盖其勢則然
也勢有所必至治有所必坊是故聖人恒
反僞以還淳斂華以復朴約繁以就簡挽
薄以從厚有其損之而莫以益也雖或益
之而意亦損也故其民易從而官亦可無
多設非不欲設自無用此贅疣爲也乃後
不識此意而以僞治僞以華治華以繁治
===
繁以薄治薄天下遂紛如矣不務反本而
多官以維持之欲以聚財財益耗欲以強
兵兵益疲欲以釐奸奸益滋欲以清刑刑
益濫求治愈急而去治則愈遠矣何者吏
議雜而自相亂也載重者恐軸之折則加
轅軸其上以爲備不知轅軸之加重而趣
軸折也佩玦而虞其破則佩兩玦以爲豫
不知兩玦相觸而破逾疾也然則多事因
以多官多官益以多事相交敝者也而多
